As for the third interpretation, it is as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal), meaning "excusing" or "warning." Both are read with light and with doubled consonants.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 77, verses 7–15:

Indeed, what you are promised of the coming of the Day of Resurrection is certainly going to happen, unavoidable, without doubt. This is the answer to the oath.

It is reported from some of them that the meaning is: "By the Sent Ones (al-mursalat)..." — ﴿ṭumisat﴾ means "effaced, erased, and annihilated." It was also said: its light is taken away and its essence is destroyed, in agreement with His words ﴿ntatharat﴾ ("scattered") and ﴿inkadarat﴾ ("darkened"). It is also possible that its light is erased and then it is scattered, erased in its light. ﴿Furijat﴾ means "opened, split," so that it becomes gates. Al-Farra' said: "the gate of an ambiguous ruler." ﴿Nusifat﴾ means "blown away like grain when it is winnowed with the winnowing shovel." Similar to this is His words: ﴿wa-bussat al-jibalu bassan﴾ ("the mountains will be crumbled to dust"), and ﴿wa-kanat al-jibalu kathiban mahilan﴾ ("the mountains will become heaps of sand, poured out"). It was also said: they are taken swiftly from their places, from "intasaftu al-shay'" when one snatches the thing away.

It is recited ﴿tumisat﴾, ﴿furijat﴾ and ﴿nusifat﴾ with the doubled letter (shaddah). It is recited ﴿uqqitat﴾ and ﴿wuqqitat﴾, with the doubling and without it in both. The original root is the waw. The meaning of the appointing (tawqit) of the Messengers is: specifying their time at which they will attend to bear witness against their nations. And ﴿ta'jil﴾ comes from ajal, just as tawqit comes from waqt. ﴿Li-ayyi yawmin ujjilat﴾ ("for what day were they postponed") is an exaltation of the Day and an expression of wonder at its terror. ﴿Li-yawmi al-fasl﴾ ("for the Day of Decision") explains the day of postponement, which is the day on which the creatures are separated. The more apt view is that the meaning of ﴿wuqqitat﴾ is: they reached their appointed time which they were awaiting, namely the Day of Resurrection. And ﴿ujjilat﴾ means: they were delayed.

If you ask: how did the indefinite noun come as the subject in His words ﴿wayln yawma'idhin lil-mukadhdhibin﴾ ("Woe on that Day to the deniers")? I answer: it is originally a verbal noun in the accusative, standing in place of its verb, but it was shifted to the nominative to indicate the continuity and permanence of destruction for the one against whom it is invoked. Similar to this is ﴿salamun 'alaykum﴾ ("Peace be upon you"). It is permissible to say ﴿waylan﴾ in the accusative, but it was not recited with it. It is said: "waylan lahu, waylan kaylan" (woe to him, woe, and sorrow).

Qatada recited "nuhlik" with a fatha on the nun, from halakahu, meaning ahlakahu (to destroy). Al-Ajjaj said: "And a deserted wasteland, destroying whoever traverses it" [the verse continues: "where the guide who knows the narrow paths cannot hope to find an exit from it"].

Al-Ajjaj. Al-mahmah is the desolate, barren wasteland. It is said: ahlakahu and halakahu. From the same root: "hāliku man taʿarraja" (destroying whoever passes through). ʿArraja and taʿarraja mean to stop and settle in a place. Al-kharīt is the guide who knows the narrow paths, even if they are as narrow as the eye of a needle. That is, the guide does not hope to find a way out once he has entered them, so how much less anyone else, even though he has traversed them by travelling.

"Thumma nutbiʿuhum" is in the nominative (rafʿ) as a resumed statement (isti'naf), and it is a warning to the people of Makkah. It means: then We will deal with the likes of them among the later ones in the same way as We dealt with the earlier ones, and We will follow with them their path, because they denied in the same manner as they denied. Reading of Ibn Masʿud supports this: "thumma sanutbiʿuhum" (then We shall certainly follow them). It was also recited in the jussive (jazm) as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "nuhlik." Its meaning: He destroyed the earlier ones, from the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud, then the later ones followed them, from the people of Shuʿayb, Lot and Musa. "Kadhalika nafʿalu bi-kulli man ajram" (Thus do We deal with everyone who commits crime), such a monstrous deed, as a warning and admonition about the consequence of crime and its evil effect.

"Unto an appointed term" (ila qadarin ma'lum): unto a known measure of time, which God knew and decreed, namely nine months, or less, or more. "Then We determined it" (faqadarna): We measured it out, determining it with a determination. "How excellent are the determiners" (fa-ni'ma al-qadirun): how excellent are We as those who determine it. Or: We had power over it, so how excellent are We as those who have power over it. The first is preferable, because of the reading of those who recite faqaddarna with the doubled letter (qaddara), and because of His saying: ﴿From a drop of fluid He created him and determined him﴾ (min nutfatin khalaqahu faqaddarahu).

Al-Kafat (the gatherer, that which gathers and holds together): from "kafata al-shay'" when one gathers and draws a thing together. It is a noun for that which gathers, like the saying "al-dimam" and "al-jima'" for what gathers and joins together; one says, "This chapter is the jima' of the chapters." By it is put in the accusative "ahyaan wa amwatan" (living and dead), as if it were said: "a gatherer of living and dead." Or it is put in the accusative by a hidden verb that indicates it, which is "takfit" (it gathers). The meaning: it gathers the living upon its surface and the dead within its belly. Some of the companions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, have used this as evidence for the amputation of the hand of the grave-robber (al-nabbash), since Allah the Exalted made the earth a gatherer for the dead, so its interior is a protected place (hirz) for them, and the grave-robber is a thief who steals from a protected place.

If you say: Why are "ahyaan" and "amwatan" stated in indefinite form, when the earth is the gatherer of the living and the dead together? I say: it is indefinite of magnification (tankir al-tafkhim), as if it were said: it gathers living ones who cannot be counted and dead ones who cannot be enumerated; and the living and dead of mankind are not all of the living and dead. It is also possible that the meaning is: it gathers you, living and dead, so that the two are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) from the pronoun, since it is known that it is a gatherer of mankind.

And it may be for magnification.

It is said to them: "Go forth to that which you used to deny, the punishment." "Go forth" is repeated.

And when it is said to them, "Eat and enjoy yourselves" — this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) describing the disbelievers: woe is established for them at the very time it is said to them, "Eat and enjoy yourselves." If you ask: how is it valid to say this to them in the Hereafter? I answer: it is said to them in the Hereafter to indicate that in the world they were deserving of being told this, and were of its people, as a reminder of their vile state and of what they brought upon themselves by preferring fleeting enjoyment over everlasting bliss and eternal dominion. In the same vein is his saying:

"My brothers, do not be far away forever..."
"...and by God, they have indeed gone far."

[The explanation of this verse was given earlier, in the second volume, p. 405; refer to it if you wish. — its corrector.]

He means: you were deserving, in your lives, of having this said for you; and he gives as the reason that they are criminals, indicating that every criminal has nothing but eating and enjoying for a few days, and then remaining in destruction forever. It is also permissible that "Eat and enjoy yourselves" be an independent statement, addressed to the disbelievers in the world.

"Bow down" (irkaʿū): submit humbly to God and show humility to Him by accepting His revelation and following His religion, and cast off this arrogance and pride. They do not bow down, nor do they accept that; they persist in their arrogance.

I answer: it is said to them in the Hereafter to indicate that in the world they were deserving of being told this, and were of its people, as a reminder of their vile state and of what they brought upon themselves by preferring fleeting enjoyment over everlasting bliss and eternal dominion. In the same vein is his saying:

"My brothers, do not be far away forever..."
"...and by God, they have indeed gone far."

[The explanation of this verse was given earlier, in the second volume, p. 405; refer to it if you wish. — its corrector.]

He means: you were deserving, in your lives, of having this said for you; and he gives as the reason that they are criminals, indicating that every criminal has nothing but eating and enjoying for a few days, and then remaining in destruction forever. It is also permissible that "Eat and enjoy yourselves" be an independent statement, addressed to the disbelievers in the world.

"Bow down" (irkaʿū): submit humbly to God and show humility to Him by accepting His revelation and following His religion, and cast off this arrogance and pride. They do not bow down, nor do they accept that; they persist in their arrogance.

It was said: nothing was harder for the Arabs than ruku' and sujud. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqīf, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded them to pray, and they said: "We will not bow (nujabbi), for it is a disgrace upon us." [Nujabbi is from tajbiyah, which is bending the back. — (ʿ)] [This is how al-Tha'labi related it. Abu Dawud, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani transmitted it from the narration of al-Hasan from ʿUthman ibn Abi al-ʿAs, and more complete than this.]

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no good in a religion that has no ruku' or sujud in it." Ba'dahu, "after it," means after the Qur'an: that is, the Qur'an among the revealed books is a clear sign and a dazzling miracle; so when they did not believe in it, in what book after it will they believe? It is also read as "tu'minūn" with the letter ta' (you believe).

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah Al-Mursalat, it is written for him that he is not among the polytheists." [Related by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh from Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
